newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper fires armed forces hawk.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper fires armed forces hawk.

text.p: The head of Colombia's armed forces, Gen. Harold Bedoya, was fired on Thursday for "reasons of state" in a surprise reshuffle following a series of public disagreements with President Ernesto Samper.

But confusion over the move grew late on Thursday when Bedoya issued a terse communique saying he had not been "officially" told of his dismissal and remained in his post until he was informed. He also questioned the president's motives for the decision.
It was not, however, immediately clear whether the general, who enjoys wide support in the ranks and is regarded as a "soldiers' soldier," was preparing to defy Samper's order.

Bedoya, a military hawk, had become increasingly vociferous in his opposition to Samper's plans to launch new peace talks with Colombia's leftist guerrillas. Samper named army chief Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett as his replacement.
"President Ernesto Samper decided today to introduce changes in the armed forces, taking into account reasons of state," Defence Minister Gilberto Echeverri said in a statement.

Bedoya issued his statement several hours later in which he said: "I have not been officially informed of any decision and as such remain for the present remain as head of the armed forces. I will not hand in my voluntary resignation."
Last month Bedoya said he would consider running for the presidency "if asked" at the conclusion of his military career.
He held the post as armed forces chief for just 8 1/2 months after being appointed last October during a guerrilla offensive.
Despite his counterinsurgency experience and training at the U.S. School of the Americas, Bedoya failed to stem the rebels.

Bedoya, whom human rights groups accused of backing right-wing death squads, consistently called for a stronger hand against the country's estimated 18,000 rebels, demanding more equipment and troops. Government ministers called instead for greater efficiency in military spending.

The military chief warned in June that Samper's proposed peace talks would allow the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Latin America's oldest and largest rebel army, to ram the "law of the jungle, the law of the strongest and most violent" down Colombia's throat.

Samper's decision to fire Bedoya comes less than a week after he firmed up his proposals to launch a state-sponsored peace process. Echeverri is due to submit a bill to Congress that will pave the way for the creation of a National Peace Council, made up of political, labour and social representatives, later this week.

In recent months graffiti has been scrawled on walls around Bogota saying: "Bedoya for president." In a radio interview in June, the outgoing armed forces chief described it as a "spontaneous" show of support for somebody who is "not prepared to hand over the country to terrorists."

Bonett, the new armed forces chief, was like Bedoya trained at the School of the Americas and has been accused of human rights violations by international and domestic organisations. Political analyst Eduardo Pizarro, however, said he was "more flexible" than Bedoya.
